title: Al-Warith, the Inheritor
hookLine: the Inheritor, to whom all returns
tomorrow: one room, one grandma, two choices. how do you pick right?

cards: Every family has the conversation nobody wants to start: who gets Grandma's ring. Some grandparents write it down and seal it. Some hand things out early, at a dinner table, and watch the faces.
Dadi has chosen early. She wants her gold bangles to go now, two to Amira, the rest to the masjid's food pantry. Amira's cousin Hana heard about it secondhand, and she is not happy.
Should Dadi wait? Inside Islam, that question has two honest answers.

teach.h: ABU BAKR: GIVE IT ALL, NOW.
teach.b: The first answer: give it now. In a hadith told by Umar, the Prophet, peace be upon him, asked for gifts for a cause, and Abu Bakr brought everything he owned.
Asked what he had left for his family, Abu Bakr said: Allah and His Messenger. Umar said he knew then he would never outdo him. Generosity, in this view, doesn't need to wait or measure.
The second answer: think of the ones you leave. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas fell ill and asked to give away most of his wealth. The Prophet said a third, and a third is a lot.

teach.h: SA'D: A THIRD; LEAVE HEIRS WELL.
teach.b: Better, he said, to leave your heirs well-off than to leave them asking people for help. Jurists drew a limit on bequests from that one conversation. So who's right?
Scholars have held both: a gift can be total, and a family's need is part of the reckoning too. Under both answers sits today's Name. Al-Warith, the Inheritor.
In Surah al-Hadid, Pickthall's words: "unto Allah belongeth the inheritance of the heavens and the earth."
Every will, early or late, ends in the same hands. What we hold, we hold on loan.

how: Muslims may give freely during life; for bequests after death, jurists set a limit drawn from the hadith of Sa'd, with the rest divided among heirs by the Qur'an's shares.

o: the Lawgiver, who writes each person's will
the Collector, who takes back what's misused
the Inheritor, to whom everything returns

games.q: two answers, one Name — tap the pairs.
p: told: a third, and a third is a lot
told the story of Abu Bakr's gift

s: in Islam, giving everything away is always the better choice
Sa'd was told a third, and that leaving heirs well-off is better. scholars hold both answers.
the Qur'an says the inheritance of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah
"unto Allah belongeth the inheritance of the heavens and the earth."

games.q: your uncle wants to give his whole savings to build a well overseas. your aunt says the kids' college comes first. what's each side's best case?
o: him: Abu Bakr gave all. her: Sa'd was told to leave heirs well-off.
her side only: giving family money away is never allowed in Islam.
his side only: holding anything back just shows weaker faith.
games.why: both have a hadith behind them, and scholars have held both. the aunt and uncle are arguing inside one tradition, not against it.

practice: Choose one thing you own that someone else would use more than you do. For the sit, make the plan: whose hands it goes to, what might stop you, and the day you'll hand it over. Hold the plan, not the thing.

wordCard.voice: Al-Warith. The Inheritor: when every owner is gone, everything is still His.

orig.note: Arabic: the Inheritor, from the traditional list of the Names; in 15:23 Allah says He is the Inheritor.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: all returns to him, the bangles, the pantry, and the ones who argue over them. Fifteen seventy-one, done.

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3675; Sunan Abi Dawud 1678 (Abu Bakr brings all his wealth, as told by Umar)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2742; Sahih Muslim 1628 (Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: a third, and a third is a lot)

sources.q: unto Allah belongeth the inheritance of the heavens and the earth
